title: Forgive before sleep
hookLine: the bedtime Shema and forgiving anyone who hurt you
tomorrow: the world stands on three things, says a sage. which fits in a day?

lines: MAR ZUTRA GOES UP TO BED.
cards: Bedtime is when the day's arguments come back for a rematch: the thing someone said, the thing you should have said back, the credit somebody else took. The lights are off and the replay is on.
The Talmud remembers a sage, Mar Zutra, who had a sentence for exactly that moment. When he went up to bed, he would say: I forgive anyone who has troubled me. That's the sentence.
Now, what it does, and what it doesn't.

teach.h: MASTER OF THE WORLD, I FORGIVE.
teach.b: Mar Zutra's line grew into a prayer. In the prayer book, before the Shema said in bed, comes a paragraph: Master of the world, I forgive anyone who angered or wronged me, in body, in money, in honor.
Then it goes further: may no one be punished because of me. The bedtime Shema itself leans on a Psalm: "commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still."
The Talmud reads that verse as the day ending with the Shema, in bed.
So the order is forgive, then hear, then sleep. What does forgiving mean here?

teach.h: MECHILAH: LETTING GO OF A CLAIM.
teach.b: The Hebrew word is mechilah, letting go of a claim, the way a lender lets go of a debt.
It isn't a verdict that what happened was fine. It doesn't require a phone call, a hug, or pretending. It's a decision about what comes to bed with you.
You can still speak up tomorrow; you just don't sleep holding the bill.
For serious harm the road is longer, and nobody is asked to pretend; the prayer is there again the next night. Something to tell a friend tonight: the prayer doesn't stop at forgiving.
It asks that the other person not be punished on your account.

how: The bedtime Shema (Kriat Shema al haMitah) is said in bed before sleep; in the prayer book it opens with a paragraph forgiving anyone who caused harm that day. Parents often say the first line of the Shema with young children at bedtime.

o: asking God to forgive your own sins each night
calling anyone you argued with before bedtime
letting go of the day's grudges before you sleep

games.q: bedtime, in order — tap the pairs.
p: I forgive anyone who troubled me
may no one be punished because of me
commune with your heart upon your bed
letting go of a claim, like a debt

s: forgiving before sleep means saying what happened was fine
mechilah lets go of a claim; it isn't a verdict, and it doesn't ask you to pretend.
the bedtime prayer asks that the other person not be punished because of you
it goes past forgiving: may no one be punished because of me.
once you've forgiven at night, you can't raise it the next day
you can still speak up tomorrow; you just don't sleep holding the bill.

games.q: your brother borrowed your car and left it on empty, again. it's 11pm and you're composing a furious text. what does the bedtime paragraph point you toward?
o: send it now, while it's fresh; forgiving means saying what you feel first.
let the claim go for tonight, sleep, and talk to him calmly tomorrow.
delete it and never mention the gas again; that's what forgiving means.
games.why: forgive, then hear, then sleep. letting go tonight isn't pretending; the conversation can still happen in daylight.

practice: Bring one small hurt from today to mind, the smallest one you can find. Say Mar Zutra's sentence quietly, in your own voice: I forgive anyone who troubled me.
Then let your shoulders drop and breathe out slowly, like setting a heavy bag down beside the bed.

wordCard.voice: Forgive before sleep: the paragraph before the bedtime Shema, letting go of the day's claims against others so they don't come to bed with you.

orig.note: Hebrew: forgiveness, letting go of a claim, as a lender lets go of a debt.

carryVoice: The line for tonight: forgive before sleeping. Tomorrow you can still speak up; tonight you put the bill down.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 28a (Mar Zutra, on going up to bed: I forgive all who troubled me)
Siddur, Kriat Shema al haMitah (the opening paragraph: Master of the world, I forgive...; may no one be punished because of me)

sources.q: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still
